name: Beef, salt and water diet

card.summary: The most restrictive carnivore variant, popularised as the lion diet: ruminant meat, salt and water only, with no controlled evidence behind it.
card.note: Supported mainly by self-reports; dietitians' bodies classify carnivore diets as fad diets and flag nutrient gaps.

quick.overview:
This is a strict elimination-style version of the carnivore diet in which a person eats only beef or other ruminant meat, salt and water. It is often called the lion diet. It became widely known through Mikhaila Peterson and her father Jordan Peterson, who described following it.

Proponents describe it as a way to identify food sensitivities and to relieve autoimmune and mood symptoms. These accounts are anecdotal; no controlled trial has tested the diet.
quick.mechanism: Advocates say removing all plant foods and most other animal foods eliminates potential triggers such as plant compounds. Near-zero carbohydrate intake means the body relies on fat and protein for energy, usually in ketosis.
quick.risks: Critics cite missing fibre and micronutrients, raised LDL cholesterol, constipation and, with high red-meat intake, associations with colon cancer and gout. Grokipedia notes that early fatigue and cramps usually fade within weeks and that scurvy has been documented in a meat-only case.

lead: The beef, salt and water diet is the strictest form of the carnivore diet: nothing is eaten except ruminant meat (mostly beef), salt and water.[1][2] It is widely called the lion diet. People who follow it do so as an elimination protocol, aiming to find out which foods trigger skin flare-ups, bloating, joint pain or low mood, and many hope that a calmer system shows up as clearer skin, less facial puffiness and a leaner, more muscular physique.[2][3]

The diet reached a mass audience through Mikhaila Peterson, who began promoting a meat-only regimen around 2018 after describing childhood-onset arthritis and later depression, and her father Jordan Peterson, who also followed it.[1][3] It later spread through social media, including TikTok.[1] Because beef is dense in protein, it is also used by some lifters and physique-focused dieters who want high protein intake with very few ingredients; a meat-only log on T Nation, for example, tracks bodyweight and training through a carnivore run.[6]

Evidence for the diet itself is limited to self-reports. Wikipedia and Grokipedia describe a 2021 self-selected survey of carnivore dieters in which most respondents reported improvement, and note that no randomised trial has tested a beef, salt and water regimen.[1][2] Dietetic organisations such as the British Dietetic Association and Dietitians Australia classify carnivore eating as a fad diet and point to fibre and micronutrient gaps.[1]

chain: Only beef, salt and water are eaten
Common trigger foods are removed and protein stays high
Practitioners report calmer skin, less bloating and a leaner physique
angle.text: Followers use the diet as a strict reset: by removing every food other than beef they hope to identify what drives skin irritation, bloating or inflammation, and they report a leaner, less puffy look as a result. Its very high protein content also appeals to people building muscle. These outcomes are described by practitioners rather than measured in trials.

paras: The diet is a minimalist subset of the carnivore diet, which allows only animal products and excludes plants.[1] In its strict form it contains ruminant meat, salt and water and nothing else, and proponents present it as an elimination protocol to identify sensitivities.[2] Looser versions add poultry, fish, eggs or low-lactose dairy.[2] Carnivore variants are often described as high-protein, high-fat and near zero-carbohydrate.[1]

People who follow the diet for their looks usually cite three aims. The first is skin: followers report fewer breakouts, less redness and less irritation once plant foods and other common triggers are removed, which is the central promise of the elimination approach.[2] The second is body composition: a meat-only intake is high in protein, and trials comparing whole-food omnivorous and vegan meals have found higher muscle protein synthesis after the omnivorous meal in older adults, a finding carnivore advocates point to when describing animal protein as anabolic.[4] The third is facial leanness, which dieters link to reduced bloating and water retention, an effect reported anecdotally rather than measured.[6]

Earlier meat-heavy regimens include the 1856 book of Bernard Moncriff, the 1870s diabetes diets of Arnaldo Cantani and James H. Salisbury's 1880s lean beef and hot water diet.[1] Grokipedia also points to Vilhjalmur Stefansson's medically observed meat-only year at Bellevue Hospital in 1928 and 1929 as a key historical reference.[2]

Wikipedia reports that the modern carnivore diet drew attention in 2018, when former surgeon Shawn Baker promoted it online and Jordan and Mikhaila Peterson adopted the lion diet, which later became a TikTok trend.[1] Mikhaila Peterson wrote that she had arthritis from age two, depression as a teenager and hip and ankle replacements at 17, and in 2018 posted a caption crediting 'beef, salt, water and bourbon' for her recovery.[3] Her site liondiet.com carries her written material, and The Guardian reported on her brief private consultations.[3] A 2023 comment from neurologist Steven Novella, cited by Wikipedia, called it the latest fad diet and noted its high cost.[1]

Advocates claim relief of autoimmune, digestive, skin and mood problems, attributing this to removal of plant compounds such as lectins and oxalates; Grokipedia describes these claims as largely anecdotal.[2] A 2021 survey of 2,029 carnivore dieters found that 95 percent reported overall improvement, but Grokipedia stresses the sample was self-selected and unvalidated.[2]

Nutrition professionals describe the carnivore diet as a fad diet; the British Dietetic Association and Dietitians Australia are among bodies that classify it that way.[1] Cited concerns include lack of dietary fibre, vitamin deficiencies from excluding fruit and vegetables, raised LDL cholesterol, constipation, and links between high red-meat intake and colon cancer, gout and kidney strain.[1]

Grokipedia lists possible shortfalls of vitamin C, folate, magnesium, potassium, calcium, thiamin and iodine, a documented scurvy case in a man eating mostly canned beef, and protein toxicity (rabbit starvation) with very lean meat. It also describes transient early fatigue and cramps ('carnivore flu') attributed to electrolyte loss.[2]

Meat-only eating is discussed on T Nation by lifters who log carnivore runs with bodyweight and training notes.[6] In one thread, a poster describes beef, salt and water as 'a form of an elimination diet' when advising another member on restarting from simple foods.[7] On looksmax.org, beef organs such as liver are promoted in long threads as nutrient-dense foods, a related but separate practice from the strict lion diet.[5]

No studies found. No controlled trial has tested a beef, salt and water diet. Related evidence for the wider carnivore diet consists of a 2021 self-selected survey, case reports and small series.[2] Separate randomised work on protein sources, such as a 2024 trial in older adults comparing omnivorous and vegan meals, measured muscle protein synthesis rather than carnivore eating.[4]

timeline.event: Bernard Moncriff's book promotes an exclusively animal diet.[1]
James H. Salisbury promotes a lean beef and hot water diet.[1]
Vilhjalmur Stefansson's supervised meat-only year begins at Bellevue Hospital.[2]
Mikhaila Peterson creates the lion diet as an elimination protocol (per Grokipedia).[2]
Mikhaila Peterson posts about her beef-only diet and the approach gains media attention.[1][3]

lore.intro: Communities describe the diet as an elimination protocol, an extreme carnivore challenge and, among lifters, a simple high-protein structure.[2][6][7]

claims.claim: Eating only beef, salt and water resolves autoimmune and mood problems.
claims.believers: Proponents, led by Mikhaila Peterson, say removing everything but ruminant meat identifies trigger foods and relieves arthritis and depression.[2][3]
claims.experts: Grokipedia describes the evidence as largely anecdotal, with no large randomised trials, and dietetic bodies classify carnivore diets as fad diets.[1][2]

claims.claim: A meat-only diet clears skin and leans out the face and body.
claims.believers: Followers report fewer breakouts and a less puffy look after dropping plant foods and dairy, and lifters report keeping muscle while cutting.[6]
claims.experts: No published trial has measured skin or facial changes on this diet; research on protein and muscle concerns protein sources in general.[4]

claims.claim: Humans do not need plant foods.
claims.believers: Advocates point to traditional animal-heavy diets such as those of the Inuit, Maasai and Plains peoples.[2]
claims.experts: Critics cite missing fibre and micronutrients and a documented scurvy case, and the diet is flagged for raised LDL cholesterol and long-term uncertainty.[1][2]
